C1 cannot explain the new pulmonary findings as an isolated pain crisis, and C2 is weakened by the focal infiltrate and explicit absence of jugular venous distention and peripheral edema. selectionEvidence: C3: Sickle cell disease plus a new pulmonary infiltrate, cough, dyspnea, tachypnea, crackles, and hypoxemia supports acute chest syndrome.
A3: The prescribed cephalosporin/macrolide regimen and supplemental oxygen address a possible infectious trigger and the current hypoxemia.
A4: Available respiratory care supports incentive spirometry and pulmonary hygiene to improve ventilation and reduce atelectatic progression.
P2: SpO₂, respiratory rate, work of breathing, and bronchospasm directly track pulmonary deterioration or improvement.
P4: Hemoglobin trend and serial assessment of infiltrate progression evaluate important hematologic and radiographic features of acute chest syndrome.
